extracted.intended_audience: plant breeders, variety developers, seed sellers, extension agents, and farmers in the United States
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the Plant Variety Protection Act (PVPA) including what it protects, available protection options, infringements, labeling/notification rules, farmer exemptions, penalties, and term lengths for protected plant varieties in the U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive rights to sell or advertise for seeding purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Varieties protected under the PVP can only be sold or advertised for seeding purposes by the protection certificate’s owner or with the owner’s permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The certificate owner may bring civil action against persons infringing on his or her rights, and may ask a court to issue an injunction to prevent others from violating proprietary rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term of protection
rubrics_metrics.description: The term of the protection expires 18 years after the certificate was issued for varieties filed before April 4, 1994, and 20 years after the certificate was issued for varieties covered under the amended act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The amended PVPA (1995) expanded coverage (e.g., potatoes and other tubers) and enabled U.S. accession to international protection frameworks (UPOV).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies and damages for infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages awarded by a court must at least compensate the certificate owner for the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awards may include attorney fees and up to triple damages if willful infringement is found; courts may also issue injunctions to stop violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Option 1 — Civil recourse (choice of protection)
rubrics_metrics.description: This option enables the developer and certificate-holder to sell certified or uncertified seed of the variety. If certificate holders’ rights are infringed upon within the period of protection, they must resort to civil action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certificate holders aren’t covered under Title V of the Federal Seed Act and violators can’t be prosecuted by the federal or state government. Similar to patent rights, certificate holders can authorize the use of their varieties on a royalty or fee basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Option 2 — Certification-only protection (choice of protection)
rubrics_metrics.description: The certification-only option uses the provision of Title V of the Federal Seed Act; the federal or state government may prosecute violators of these laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A variety protected in this manner may only be sold as a class of certified seed. Sales of uncertified seed by variety name is a violation of the certificate owner’s rights and federal and state seed laws. Violations of any provision, rule or regulation of the Federal Seed Act is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine not to exceed $2,000. Farmers who wish to produce seed of protected varieties for sale must get authorization from the certificate’s owner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts constituting infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed acts that, when performed without the certificate owner’s authority, constitute infringement of the owner’s rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: using seed marketed as “unauthorized propagation prohibited” to produce seed of the variety to market for growing purposes; selling or advertising a protected variety; distributing the variety to another person without informing them the variety is protected; importing the variety into the United States or exporting it; including a third party to commit any of the above acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional rules for varieties with Certificates issued after April 4, 1994
rubrics_metrics.description: Varieties whose Certificate of Protection was issued under the amended act after April 4, 1994 are subject to further regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seed-protected varieties must be sold by variety name. Conditioners who knowingly clean seed of protected varieties for sale are subject to the same penalties imposed on the seed sellers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seller notification and labeling requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s the seller’s responsibility to inform the buyer if a variety is protected. Seed containers should be labeled indicating the type of protection the owner has applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the variety owner chooses to sell either uncertified or certified seed, the label should state, “unauthorized propagation prohibited – U.S. protected variety.” This statement, or others similar to it as defined in the act, is sufficient notification of protection. If the seed is purchased in bulk, the appropriate statement should be printed on the bulk sales certificate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Farmer exemption (saved seed clause)
rubrics_metrics.description: The original PVPA specifies a farmer exemption in the “saved seed” clause for growers who aren’t involved with producing crops for seeding purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exemption applies to varieties protected by PVPA and to varieties protected under the certification-only option of the Federal Seed Act whose Certificate of Protection was issued before April 4, 1996. Farmers whose primary occupation is producing crops for food or feed and who’ve obtained seed of a variety protected under the original act may save seed for their own use from personal crop production, or sell a certain amount to another farmer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity limit on seed sales under the farmer exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of seed that can be sold under the farmer exemption is limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per U.S. Supreme Court case Asgrow v. Winterboer, the amount is no greater than the amount of seed the grower originally planted to produce the seed crop. This exemption doesn’t cover varieties whose certificate of protection was issued after April 4, 1994, so seed sales of these varieties aren’t allowed without the certificate holder’s permission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditioners' liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Conditioners who knowingly clean seed of protected varieties for sale may be liable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For seed-protected varieties (post-amendment), conditioners who knowingly clean seed of protected varieties for sale are subject to the same penalties imposed on the seed sellers.

rubrics_metrics.name: International protection recognition (UPOV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments to the PVPA allowed the United States to be a signatory in the International Convention for the Protection of New Varieties of Plants (UPOV).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This membership ensures proprietary rights on varieties are respected in many countries worldwide.
